ladakh.name: Ladakh
ladakh.subtitle: The Indus valley, between the Karakoram and the Great Himalaya
ladakh.geology:
How the ground got here

Ladakh sits directly on the Indus–Yarlung suture — the welded seam where the Indian plate finished colliding with Asia around 50 million years ago. The Tethys Ocean used to be here. Its floor was scraped off and stacked into the ridges north of the river; you can find marine fossils and slabs of ancient ocean crust within sight of the road.

The pale granite spine of the Ladakh Range is the eroded root of a volcanic arc that once stood above that vanished ocean, the way the Andes stand above the Pacific today. The Indus, older than the mountains it cuts through, kept sawing downward as the range rose around it — which is why the valley runs along the seam instead of across it.

Everything here is high desert: 3,000–5,500 m, under 100 mm of rain a year. The Himalaya to the south takes the monsoon before it arrives. Water comes from snow and ice, not sky.

entries.title: Ice, and the edge of the possible
entries.body:
For most of this stretch Ladakh is at or beyond the limit of where people can live. Glaciers push far down the valleys; the plateau above is cold desert.

The Tibetan Plateau was reached earlier than anyone expected — the site of Nwya Devu in central Tibet puts people at 4,600 m somewhere between 40,000 and 30,000 years ago. Ladakh's own Palaeolithic record is thin and hard to date: scattered stone tools, and no securely excavated deep sequence yet.

What Ladakh does have, in extraordinary quantity, is rock art. Thousands of figures are pecked into desert-varnished boulders along the Indus at Domkhar, Khaltse and Alchi — ibex above all, plus hunters, chariots, stupas and later inscriptions. The earliest phases are usually placed in the Neolithic or Bronze Age rather than the Palaeolithic, but the sequence runs for millennia, which makes it one of the longest continuous conversations any people has had with a single set of rocks.

Dating rock art is notoriously slippery. Treat the early end of these ranges as argued, not settled.

entries.title: Herders on the Changthang
entries.body:
Pastoralism, not farming, is what makes this landscape workable — and the pattern established here has held for thousands of years.

The Changthang, the high plain running east into Tibet, supports a nomadic herding economy built on yak, sheep and the goat whose winter undercoat becomes pashmina. Where the Indus and its tributaries widen, small irrigated pockets allow barley — the crop that made settled life at this altitude possible at all.

The ibex carvings multiply through this period. So do chariots, which is interesting: a wheeled vehicle in a valley where wheels are close to useless suggests contact with steppe cultures to the north rather than local use.

entries.title: Mon and Dard: the remembered predecessors
entries.body:
Ladakhi tradition holds that two populations were here before the Tibetans: the Mon and the Dards.

The Dards are Indo-Aryan speakers who came up the Indus from the west, from Gilgit and Baltistan. Their descendants — the Brokpa of Dha, Hanu and Garkone in the lower Indus gorge — still speak a Shina-related language and keep distinct rituals, dress and marriage customs.

"Mon" is fuzzier: in Ladakhi usage it names an earlier people, and today also a musician caste. Whether it once described a specific population or was a general Tibetan word for lowlanders is genuinely unresolved.

This is a period where oral tradition, later chronicles and thin archaeology disagree. The shape is right; the details are contested.

entries.title: A crossroads finds the Buddha
entries.body:
Buddhism arrives from the west — from Kashmir and Gandhara, not from Tibet, which has not yet converted.

Ladakh sits where four worlds touch: Kashmir and the Indian plains to the south, Baltistan and Central Asia to the west and north, the Tarim oases of Khotan and Kashgar beyond the Karakoram, and the Tibetan plateau to the east. Kushan-era material turns up here; so do rock-cut Maitreya figures at Mulbekh and Kartse in a plainly Gandharan idiom.

Nothing about Ladakh's later Tibetan character was inevitable. For centuries its cultural gravity pulled west and south.

entries.title: The Tibetan Empire arrives — and everything changes
entries.body:
This is the decisive event in Ladakh's history. It stops being a Dardic-Indic borderland and becomes Tibetan.

From the mid-7th century the Tibetan Empire expands explosively out of the Yarlung valley, taking the western plateau and pushing into the Tarim Basin, where it fights the Tang for control of the Silk Road oases. Ladakh is absorbed. The Tibetan language, the Tibetan script, and eventually Tibetan Buddhism all arrive with imperial administration.

Then in 842 the empire disintegrates after the assassination of Langdarma. The centre collapses; the periphery is left holding the culture.

entries.title: Maryul, and a second beginning for Buddhism
entries.body:
Out of the empire's wreckage, a great-grandson of Langdarma named Nyima-Gon moves west and founds a kingdom in Ladakh. It is called Maryul — 'the lowland' — and it is the ancestor of every Ladakhi state since.

What follows is the phyi dar, the 'later diffusion' of Buddhism, and western Tibet is its engine. The translator Rinchen Zangpo (958–1055) is sent to Kashmir, returns with texts and with Kashmiri artists, and is credited with founding monasteries across Ladakh, Zanskar and Spiti.

The murals at Alchi Choskhor, painted between roughly the 11th and 13th centuries, are the reason art historians come here. They are Kashmiri in style — the last substantial survival of a tradition that was destroyed in Kashmir itself.

entries.title: The Namgyal kings and the Lion
entries.body:
Ladakh's high-water mark as an independent power.

The Namgyal dynasty is founded around 1460 by Lhachen Bhagan, who reunites a fragmented kingdom. Islam has by now reached Ladakh along the Kashmir trade route and taken firm root downstream in Baltistan and around Kargil — Ladakh becomes, and remains, religiously mixed.

The peak is Sengge Namgyal (r. c. 1616–1642), the 'Lion King', who pushes Ladakh's reach across western Tibet and builds on a scale the kingdom never matched again: the nine-storey palace above Leh, and the monastery at Hemis.

entries.title: A war over Tibet, and a treaty about wool
entries.body:
Ladakh overreaches, loses, and is permanently reduced — by a peace treaty about goat hair.

Ladakhi involvement in Tibetan sectarian politics triggers the Tibet–Ladakh–Mughal war of 1679–1684. Ladakh is invaded, and buys Mughal help from Kashmir at a lasting price. The Treaty of Tingmosgang (1684) fixes the Ladakh–Tibet boundary near Demchok, bars Ladakh from Tibetan affairs, and — the clause that mattered — routes the pashmina wool of western Tibet through Ladakh to Kashmir and nowhere else.

That single commercial clause fed the Kashmir shawl industry, which fed a European fashion craze, which is a reason the British later cared about who controlled these valleys at all.

entries.title: Conquest by Jammu, and a border problem that outlives everyone
entries.body:
Between 1834 and 1842, the Dogra general Zorawar Singh — serving Gulab Singh of Jammu — conquers Ladakh, then Baltistan, then marches into western Tibet, where he is killed at Toyo in 1841.

Ladakh's independence ends. The 1846 Treaty of Amritsar makes Gulab Singh maharaja of the new princely state of Jammu and Kashmir under British paramountcy, with Ladakh inside it. British surveyors and Moravian missionaries follow; the Leh mission opens in 1885.

The boundary with Tibet is never properly demarcated on the ground. It is a small omission with a very long tail.

entries.title: The routes close
entries.body:
Partition, then two wars, turn a crossroads into a cul-de-sac.

Ladakh becomes part of Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in 1947–48. The 1950s close the Tibet trade; the caravan roads to Yarkand and Lhasa that had run for a thousand years simply stop. The 1962 Sino-Indian war leaves China holding Aksai Chin, the high desert northeast of the Ladakh range, and the Line of Actual Control unsettled to this day.

Ladakh reopens to outsiders in 1974, this time as a destination rather than a corridor. In 2019 it is separated from Jammu and Kashmir and made a Union Territory in its own right.

Boundaries in this region are actively disputed between India, Pakistan and China. Any map of it — including this one — is a claim, not a fact.

sources.text: Rizvi, J. — Ladakh: Crossroads of High Asia (OUP, 1996)
Petech, L. — The Kingdom of Ladakh c. 950–1842 A.D. (IsMEO, 1977)

doggerland.name: Doggerland
doggerland.subtitle: The drowned country under the North Sea
doggerland.geology:
How the ground got here

The North Sea basin is shallow — much of it under 40 m, and Dogger Bank itself under 20. That shallowness is the whole story: a sea level fall of a hundred metres, which the ice ages delivered repeatedly, turns the entire basin into dry land.

During glacial maxima, ice locked up enough water to drop global sea level by around 125 m. Britain stopped being an island and became a peninsula of Europe, and the ground between was not a marginal land bridge but a large, low, well-watered plain crossed by the ancestral Rhine, Thames and Meuse.

The land is still moving. Scandinavia, released from its ice load, is rising; southern Britain and the Netherlands are tilting down in response. Sea level here is a moving target on both ends.

entries.title: Neanderthal country
entries.body:
Sea level swings through this period, and the basin floods and drains more than once.

During the last interglacial, around 125,000 years ago, the sea stood a few metres higher than today and Britain was firmly an island. As the climate cooled again the water withdrew and the plain reopened.

Neanderthals were here. In 2009 a fragment of a Neanderthal skull was identified among material dredged from the Zeeland Ridges off the Dutch coast — the first Neanderthal fossil recovered from the North Sea floor.

entries.title: The Last Glacial Maximum
entries.body:
The coldest point, around 20,000 BCE. The map you are looking at is at its most unfamiliar.

An ice sheet covers Scandinavia and much of Britain. Sea level is roughly 125 m below today's. The southern North Sea is a treeless polar desert of tundra and steppe, cut by braided rivers; the Channel is a valley, not a strait.

Scrub the timeline across this period and watch the shelf come up dry: not just here, but Sundaland between Borneo and Malaya, Beringia between Siberia and Alaska, and the land that joined New Guinea to Australia. All of them appear at once, because all of them are the same shallow-shelf effect.

Human occupation of northern Europe at the maximum is sparse to absent. People are further south, in refugia in Iberia and the Balkans, and will move back north as the ice releases.

entries.title: The richest place in Europe
entries.body:
Warming is fast. Tundra becomes birch, then pine and hazel woodland. Reindeer give way to red deer, elk, aurochs and boar. And people come back.

This is Doggerland at its peak — a low plain of rivers, lakes, marsh, estuary and coast. Every one of those is a productive Mesolithic environment, and here they are stacked together. It was very probably better country than the uplands that survived as Britain and the Netherlands.

The evidence arrives by accident, in fishing nets. In 1931 the trawler Colinda pulled a barbed antler point out of a lump of peat off the Leman and Ower Banks — a Mesolithic hunting weapon from land that no longer exists. Trawlers still bring up mammoth, aurochs and deer bone from Dogger Bank.

Since the 2000s, Vince Gaffney's team at Bradford has mapped Doggerland's rivers, lakes and coastlines from oil-industry seismic survey data — reconstructing the topography of a drowned country without ever excavating it. Sedimentary ancient DNA is now filling in its vegetation.

entries.title: The drowning
entries.body:
Meltwater raises the sea faster than the land can rise to meet it. Doggerland goes under within a few thousand years — fast enough to be lived through.

The plain becomes an archipelago; the archipelago becomes shoals. Around 6200 BCE the Storegga Slide, an enormous submarine landslide off Norway, sends a tsunami across the northern North Sea and strikes what is left of the Dogger Bank islands, which by then are low and exposed.

By roughly 6000–5500 BCE the sea has closed behind Britain. Britain becomes an island and its later history — every invasion, every isolation, every Channel crossing — starts running on different rules.

Exact dates for the final separation are debated and keep moving as new cores are dated. Read the century figures as approximate.

entries.title: Sea
entries.body:
From here on, Doggerland exists only as bathymetry, as bone in trawl nets, and as seismic lines in an oil company's archive.

Dogger Bank stays shallow enough to be one of the great fishing grounds of Europe, and shallow enough, now, to be covered in wind turbines whose foundation surveys are quietly producing some of the best archaeology anyone has of the place.

Roughly one in ten of the world's currently inhabited coastal cities sits on ground that was dry plain, then seabed, then something in between. Doggerland is the best-studied case of a process that happened on every shallow shelf on Earth.

sources.text: Gaffney, V., Fitch, S. & Smith, D. — Europe's Lost World: The Rediscovery of Doggerland (CBA, 2009)
Weninger, B. et al. — 'The catastrophic final flooding of Doggerland by the Storegga Slide tsunami', Documenta Praehistorica 35 (2008)
Doggerland
Storegga Slide

cappadocia.name: Cappadocia
cappadocia.subtitle: Volcanic tableland in the heart of Anatolia
cappadocia.geology:
How the ground got here

Three volcanoes — Erciyes, Hasan Dağı and Göllü Dağ — buried this plateau in ash. Over roughly the last ten million years, successive eruptions laid down thick sheets of ignimbrite: welded volcanic ash, soft enough to carve with hand tools, hard enough to stand up.

Harder basalt caps protected columns of the softer tuff beneath while everything around them eroded. What survives are the peribacaları, the fairy chimneys — a landform that exists because two rock types weather at different speeds.

The same softness explains almost everything human here. If you can dig a house with a pick, you dig a house. Cappadocians have been carving dwellings, churches, stables, storerooms and entire multi-level underground cities out of this rock for at least three thousand years, and the region's dovecotes and cellars are still cut into it.

entries.title: Obsidian country
entries.body:
Before Cappadocia is anything else, it is a source of the best cutting edge available in the ancient Near East.

The volcanic complex at Göllü Dağ, and nearby Nenezi Dağ, produce obsidian — volcanic glass that fractures to an edge sharper than surgical steel. Palaeolithic groups are working it here long before farming.

Obsidian is geochemically fingerprintable, so its trade can be traced exactly. Cappadocian obsidian turns up hundreds of kilometres away, and its distribution is one of the clearest maps we have of Stone Age exchange networks.

entries.title: Aşıklı Höyük and the first villages
entries.body:
Some of the earliest settled communities anywhere are on this plateau.

Aşıklı Höyük, on the Melendiz river near Aksaray, is occupied from about 8200 BCE: a dense cluster of mudbrick houses entered through the roof, with the dead buried beneath the floors. It records, in stratigraphy, the shift from hunting to managing sheep and goats.

Cappadocian obsidian now reaches Cyprus and the southern Levant, including Jericho. Fifty kilometres southwest, Çatalhöyük becomes the largest known Neolithic settlement in the world; one of its wall paintings has long been read as a townscape beneath an erupting Hasan Dağı, which would make it the oldest landscape picture ever found.

That reading of the Çatalhöyük painting is disputed — many archaeologists see a leopard skin and a geometric pattern rather than a volcano and a map.

entries.title: Kaneš: writing arrives in a merchant's ledger
entries.body:
Anatolia's first written records are not royal proclamations. They are business correspondence.

From roughly 1950 to 1750 BCE, merchants from Aššur in northern Mesopotamia run a trading colony — a kārum — outside the Anatolian city of Kaneš, modern Kültepe near Kayseri. They bring tin and fine textiles by donkey caravan and take back silver and gold.

More than 23,000 cuneiform tablets have come out of Kültepe: contracts, loans, lawsuits, tax disputes, and letters between husbands in Anatolia and wives running the business back in Aššur. It is one of the richest windows into ordinary Bronze Age life anywhere on Earth, and it exists because a group of merchants were meticulous about their paperwork.

entries.title: Hittites, and the long unravelling
entries.body:
Cappadocia is core territory of the Hittite Empire, the Bronze Age power that fought Egypt to a draw at Kadesh and signed the earliest surviving peace treaty between two states.

The capital is Hattusa, north of here. Around 1180 BCE the empire falls apart in the general Late Bronze Age collapse that takes down half the eastern Mediterranean at once.

What survives in and around Cappadocia are the Neo-Hittite successor states — Tabal among them — writing in Luwian hieroglyphs, holding out against Assyria, and eventually absorbed.

entries.title: Katpatuka
entries.body:
The name itself is Persian. Under the Achaemenids this is the satrapy of Katpatuka, which Greek speakers render as Kappadokia and which we still say today.

The Royal Road from Sardis to Susa runs across Anatolia, and Cappadocia is horse country — the satrapy's tribute is reckoned partly in horses.

After Alexander, the region does something unusual: rather than becoming a Macedonian kingdom it stays under a local dynasty, the Ariarathids, who rule an independent Kingdom of Cappadocia for two and a half centuries while playing Seleucids, Pontus and then Rome against each other with considerable skill.

entries.title: Rome, and three theologians
entries.body:
Tiberius annexes the kingdom as a Roman province in 17 CE. Five centuries later Cappadocia is one of the most consequential places in Christian thought.

The Cappadocian Fathers — Basil of Caesarea, his brother Gregory of Nyssa, and Gregory of Nazianzus — write in the second half of the 4th century and effectively settle the Trinitarian language the Council of Constantinople adopts in 381. Basil also organises monasticism into a communal rule, and founds the Basileias, a complex outside Caesarea combining hospital, hostel and poorhouse that is often called the first hospital.

Basil's rule shaped eastern monasticism, and through it Benedict, and through Benedict most of western monasticism. That lineage starts on this plateau.

entries.title: The frontier goes underground
entries.body:
For four centuries Cappadocia is the Byzantine–Arab military frontier, raided almost annually. The response is written into the rock.

The underground complexes at Derinkuyu and Kaymaklı — earlier cuttings, dramatically enlarged in this period — descend many levels, with ventilation shafts, wells, stables, chapels, wineries and rolling stone doors that seal from the inside. They are not cities in the sense of permanent homes; they are refuges designed to hide a whole community and its animals until a raiding column moves on.

Rock-cut churches multiply across the valleys. So does a dispersed, defensible pattern of settlement that suits a landscape where the safest structure is the one you cannot see.

entries.title: Seljuk Anatolia and the painted churches
entries.body:
The Byzantine defeat at Manzikert in 1071 opens Anatolia to the Turks. Cappadocia passes to the Sultanate of Rum, ruled from Konya.

What follows is less a rupture than a long overlap. Christian communities remain, and the finest painted churches of Göreme — the Karanlık Kilise among them — belong to roughly this era, their Byzantine programmes executed under Seljuk rule.

The Seljuks build caravanserais a day's march apart along the trade roads; Sultanhanı, north of Aksaray, dates to 1229. The region is a corridor again.

entries.title: Ottoman centuries
entries.body:
Under the Ottomans Cappadocia is quiet provincial country: wine, horses, wheat, pigeon manure for the vineyards, and stone cut from the same tuff everyone has always cut.

Its Orthodox Christian population persists for another five hundred years. Many of them speak Turkish rather than Greek and write it in the Greek alphabet — the Karamanlides. Villages like Sinasos, now Mustafapaşa, grow prosperous on trade with Istanbul and build handsome stone mansions that still stand.

entries.title: An emptying, and an afterlife
entries.body:
The 1923 Greco-Turkish population exchange ends the Orthodox presence in Cappadocia after roughly two thousand years.

Whole villages are emptied and resettled by Muslims arriving from Greece. The rock churches are abandoned to pigeons and to storage; some are used as dovecotes, which is part of why their paintings survived at all.

Göreme and the surrounding valleys are inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1985. The cave dwellings that people spent three millennia carving are now, in a turn nobody could have predicted, hotel rooms.

sources.text: Rodley, L. — Cave Monasteries of Byzantine Cappadocia (CUP, 1985)
Ousterhout, R. — Visualizing Community: Art, Material Culture, and Settlement in Byzantine Cappadocia (Dumbarton Oaks, 2017)

sundaland.name: Sundaland
sundaland.subtitle: The drowned lowland between Borneo, Java and the Malay Peninsula
sundaland.geology:
How the ground got here

The Sunda Shelf is one of the largest areas of continental shelf on Earth — a shallow platform, mostly under 50 m of water, joining Borneo, Sumatra and Java to mainland Asia. Like the North Sea, its shallowness is the whole story: a glacial fall in sea level turns the entire shelf into a single lowland the size of India.

Two great river systems drained it. The North Sunda or Molengraaff river carried the ancestral Kapuas and the rivers of eastern Sumatra north into the South China Sea; a southern system ran between Sumatra and Java. Their drowned channels are still legible on the seabed.

This is tectonic frontier country. The shelf itself is stable continental crust, but its southern and eastern rim is the Sunda Arc — Krakatoa, Tambora, Toba — one of the most violent volcanic margins on the planet.

entries.title: Homo erectus, and then the ash
entries.body:
For most of the Pleistocene, low sea levels mean there is no Indonesia — only a forested peninsula of Asia.

Java has one of the longest hominin records anywhere: Homo erectus is here from perhaps 1.5 million years ago, and a late, separate species — Homo floresiensis, the 'hobbit' — persists on Flores, reachable only by a sea crossing, until around 50,000 years ago.

Around 74,000 years ago the Toba supereruption in northern Sumatra throws out roughly 2,800 km³ of material — the largest eruption of the last two million years. Ash falls centimetres deep across South Asia. Whether it caused a population bottleneck in early humans is argued hard in both directions.

The 'Toba catastrophe' hypothesis is genuinely unsettled. Some records show forests recovering within decades; others read a long volcanic winter.

entries.title: The road to Sahul
entries.body:
Modern humans move through here on the way to Australia — and they do it while Sundaland is dry and Sahul, to the southeast, is a single continent joining Australia to New Guinea.

Even at the lowest sea level, the crossing is never fully closed: a chain of straits — Wallace's Line — always separates Sundaland's Asian animals from Australia's marsupials. People cross it by around 65,000–50,000 years ago, in what are, on any reading, deliberate open-water voyages. It is the earliest solid evidence of boats anywhere.

The animals never made the jump: no tigers, monkeys or elephants ever reached Australia; no kangaroos or cockatoos ever reached Borneo. People are the exception that proves how real the water gap was.

entries.title: A continent at its fullest, then the flood
entries.body:
At the Last Glacial Maximum, Sundaland is a lowland plain of rainforest, savanna mosaic, rivers and freshwater swamp — and then, over ten thousand years, it drowns.

As the ice melts, the sea rises across an almost flat surface, so it advances fast and far: a metre of rise can move the coastline kilometres inland. The plain breaks into the islands we know. Some researchers argue this drowning scattered a lowland population outward — carrying language, crops and story — and read the flood myths of the region as a memory of it. Others see ordinary Holocene sea-level rise and caution against turning it into an Atlantis.

The 'Sundaland as cradle of civilisation' claim (associated with Oppenheimer's Eden in the East) is not the mainstream view. The drowning is real and dramatic; the grand diffusionist story built on it is not established.

entries.title: Islands, and the people who would leave them
entries.body:
Sundaland is now an archipelago. Its people are hunter-gatherers and, increasingly, gardeners of yam, taro, banana and sago.

From around 4,000 BCE, Austronesian-speaking farmers spread south out of Taiwan through the Philippines and into this archipelago, bringing rice, pigs, pottery and outrigger canoes. Over the next few thousand years their descendants will settle an ocean — from Madagascar to Easter Island to New Zealand — in the widest pre-modern expansion of any language family.

The drowned shelf becomes the maritime world of the Nusantara: short crossings, monsoon timing, trade in forest products, and eventually the Hindu-Buddhist and then Muslim polities of Srivijaya, Majapahit and the Malacca sultanate.

entries.title: Sea, and shelf again
entries.body:
From here on the map is the modern one. What was a continent is the world's largest archipelagic nation and a set of busy shallow seas.

The drowned lowland is still shaping things. The shelf's shallowness makes it one of the most productive fishing grounds and one of the most exposed coastlines on Earth: a large fraction of Jakarta sits on subsiding former swamp, and the government has begun moving the capital to higher ground on Borneo.

Trawlers and dredgers off Sumatra and around the Riau islands still bring up the teeth and bones of Pleistocene elephants, rhinos and deer — surface finds from a plain that has been underwater for nine thousand years.

sources.text: Bellwood, P. — Prehistory of the Indo-Malaysian Archipelago (ANU Press, rev. 2007)
Hanebuth, T., Stattegger, K. & Grootes, P. — 'Rapid flooding of the Sunda Shelf', Science 288 (2000)
Sundaland

mesopotamia.name: Southern Mesopotamia
mesopotamia.subtitle: The alluvium between the Tigris and Euphrates, near Uruk
mesopotamia.geology:
How the ground got here

This is one of the youngest landscapes on Earth to carry a great civilisation. Every bit of it is river sediment — silt dropped by the Tigris and Euphrates as they slow on their way to the Gulf — laid down over the last ten thousand years on top of a slowly sinking basin, the foreland trough where the Arabian plate dives under the Zagros.

Because the land is flat and the rivers are higher than the plain between them, they wander and jump their banks. Cities that sat on a channel could be left dry by a shift of a few kilometres; the ruin of Uruk is now well out in the desert, nowhere near the modern Euphrates.

The head of the Gulf has moved. In the early Holocene the shoreline reached much further inland, and Ur and Eridu were near-coastal. Millennia of silt have since pushed the land seaward past Basra.

entries.title: Marsh, and no one to see it
entries.body:
For most of prehistory this plain does not exist. Through the last glacial period sea level is 120 m down, the Gulf is a dry valley with the combined river running along it, and the future heartland of cities is a windswept lowland.

As the ice melts the sea floods back up the valley, drowning the river plain and creating, at its inland edge, an enormous zone of reed marsh, lagoon and shifting channel. Small groups of foragers and fishers are present around the margins, but the alluvium proper is still forming.

entries.title: The Ubaid: learning to farm a floodplain
entries.body:
The first villages on the southern alluvium belong to the Ubaid culture, and their achievement is hydraulic: the plain gets under 200 mm of rain, so every field has to be irrigated.

Small canals tap the river; barley and date palm do the work; sheep and goat graze the fallow. Eridu, later remembered by the Sumerians as the first city of all, begins as an Ubaid shrine rebuilt on the same spot again and again.

Ubaid pottery and the boat-borne trade that carried it spread the whole length of the Gulf and up into northern Mesopotamia — a shared material world stretching a thousand kilometres before there is a single king.

entries.title: Uruk: the first city on Earth
entries.body:
Between roughly 3800 and 3100 BCE, Uruk becomes something the world has not had before — a city of tens of thousands, drawing in people and grain from its whole hinterland.

Everything associated with early states appears here in a rush: monumental temple platforms, mass-produced ration bowls, cylinder seals, the specialised potter's wheel, and — to track all the grain moving through the temple stores — writing, beginning as accounting marks pressed into clay around 3300 BCE.

The earliest tablets are not literature or law. They are receipts: quantities of barley, beer, sheep and labour. Literature comes centuries later, once the system exists.

Uruk-style colonies and outposts spring up hundreds of kilometres away along the trade routes north — the first time a southern lowland reaches out and reorganises its neighbours.

entries.title: Sumer and Akkad: cities, then empire
entries.body:
The plain fills with rival city-states — Ur, Uruk, Lagash, Umma, Kish, Nippur — each with its patron god, its temple, its king, and its endless border war with the next one over water.

Around 2334 BCE Sargon of Akkad conquers all of them and builds the first empire anyone would recognise as such: a standing army, appointed governors, his daughter Enheduanna installed as high priestess at Ur and writing the earliest poetry attributed to a named author.

It does not hold. The Akkadian empire collapses within a few generations — drought is one suspected cause — is briefly rebuilt by the Third Dynasty of Ur with a bureaucracy of staggering thoroughness, and collapses again.

entries.title: Babylon, and the slow poisoning of the fields
entries.body:
Hammurabi's Babylon (c. 1792–1750 BCE) makes the city the lasting centre of the south, a status it keeps under Kassites, Assyrians and the Neo-Babylonian kings for over a thousand years.

But the land itself is tiring. Irrigating a hot floodplain with no natural drainage pulls salt to the surface; over centuries the southern fields shift from wheat to salt-tolerant barley and then, in places, go out of cultivation entirely. The centre of gravity drifts north toward Babylon and Baghdad, where it has stayed.

How much salinisation drove Sumer's decline versus war, siltation and canal politics is debated. It was clearly one real pressure among several.

entries.title: Provinces, and marshes
entries.body:
After Cyrus takes Babylon in 539 BCE the south is a province — Persian, then Seleucid, Parthian, Sasanian, and from 637 CE Islamic, ruled from Ctesiphon and then nearby Baghdad.

The extreme south reverts to what it was before the cities: the Ahwar, the great marshes, home to the Maʻdan who build reed houses on floating islands in a way strikingly close to the Sumerian images. Saddam Hussein's regime drained most of the marshes in the 1990s as a reprisal; partial reflooding since 2003 has brought some of them back.

The World Heritage listing for the region, made in 2016, is a joint one: the marshes and the ruined cities — Uruk, Ur, Eridu — named together, as one drowned-and-resurfaced landscape.

sources.text: Van De Mieroop, M. — A History of the Ancient Near East (Wiley-Blackwell, 3rd ed. 2015)

great-zimbabwe.name: Great Zimbabwe
great-zimbabwe.subtitle: Stone city on the Zimbabwe plateau, between the Limpopo and the Zambezi
great-zimbabwe.geology:
How the ground got here

The Zimbabwe Craton is very old continental crust — over 2.5 billion years — and its granite weathers in a particular way: onion-skin exfoliation peels off curved sheets, leaving rounded kopjes and, crucially, natural slabs that split into flat, brick-like blocks along the sheeting planes.

That is the building material. The dry-stone walls of Great Zimbabwe — no mortar, some over 5 m thick and 11 m high — are made of granite that the hill quarried for the builders by cracking in the sun and frost.

The plateau sits high enough (1,000–1,500 m) to be cool, well-watered and free of the tsetse fly that makes cattle-keeping impossible in the lowveld on either side. Everything about the site's wealth starts with that: it is good cattle country next to gold country.

entries.title: Foragers, and the first farmers
entries.body:
The plateau has one of the richest concentrations of hunter-gatherer rock art in the world — fine polychrome paintings by the ancestors of the San, spanning many thousands of years.

In the first few centuries CE, Bantu-speaking farmers move onto the plateau from the north, bringing sorghum and millet, cattle, and — soon — iron working. The forager and farmer worlds overlap for a long time before the farming economy becomes dominant.

entries.title: Cattle, chiefs and the Indian Ocean
entries.body:
By the later first millennium, plateau societies are stratified: cattle are wealth, wealth is political power, and the hilltop is where the powerful live.

At Mapungubwe, just south on the Limpopo, a class of rulers physically separates itself onto a sandstone hill around 1220 CE, buried with gold ornaments — a gold rhino, gold bangles — and Chinese celadon and glass beads from the coast. This is the template Great Zimbabwe scales up: sacred leadership, cattle, and a trade route running to the Swahili port of Sofala and out into the monsoon world.

entries.title: The city at its height
entries.body:
Between roughly 1100 and 1450 CE, Great Zimbabwe is the largest settlement in sub-Saharan Africa outside the Nile — perhaps 18,000 people at its peak, spread across several square kilometres.

The stone enclosures — the Hill Complex, the Great Enclosure with its mysterious conical tower, the Valley ruins — are built for the elite; most people live in daga (earth and clay) houses around them. The economy runs on cattle, farmed grain, ironwork, and above all gold, panned and mined across the plateau and traded to the coast for cloth, ceramics and glass beads. Persian and Chinese pottery has been excavated inside the walls.

The soapstone birds found on the site — eight carved raptors on tall columns — are unique to Great Zimbabwe. One of them is the emblem on the flag of the modern country, which took the ruin's name at independence in 1980.

entries.title: Moved on, not fallen
entries.body:
Great Zimbabwe is largely abandoned in the 15th century — probably because a city that size exhausts its firewood, grazing and soil, and the trade and the rulers shift elsewhere.

Elsewhere means the Mutapa state to the north, near the Zambezi, and the Torwa and later Rozvi states to the southwest at Khami and Danangombe, which keep building in dressed stone — often more finely than Great Zimbabwe itself. The tradition does not end; its centre relocates.

When the Portuguese arrive on the Zambezi in the 1500s they trade with, and write about, the Mutapa court — one of the few African interior states documented from the outside this early.

entries.title: A ruin, and an argument about who built it
entries.body:
From the moment Europeans reached the site in the 1870s, colonial society insisted Africans could not have built it — proposing Phoenicians, Arabs, the Queen of Sheba, anyone else.

Early treasure-hunters, licensed by Cecil Rhodes's company, wrecked the archaeology digging for gold. Careful excavation — by David Randall-MacIver in 1905, Gertrude Caton-Thompson in 1929, and everyone since — showed unambiguously that the builders were the local Shona ancestors, from the medieval period. The Rhodesian government suppressed that conclusion into the 1970s.

The site is now a UNESCO World Heritage listing and a national symbol. The dispute over its origins is a case study, taught worldwide, in how politics bends archaeology.

Population and date figures for the city vary between researchers. The identity of the builders does not — that is settled.

sources.text: Pikirayi, I. — The Zimbabwe Culture: Origins and Decline of Southern Zambezian States (AltaMira, 2001)
Huffman, T. N. — Snakes and Crocodiles: Power and Symbolism in Ancient Zimbabwe (Wits UP, 1996)

cahokia.name: Cahokia
cahokia.subtitle: Earthwork city in the Mississippi floodplain, opposite modern St. Louis
cahokia.geology:
How the ground got here

Cahokia sits in the American Bottom, a wide belt of Mississippi River floodplain below the confluence with the Missouri and Illinois. The river has spent the last ten thousand years swinging back and forth across this bottomland, leaving a patchwork of old channels, oxbow lakes, natural levees and rich backswamp — an unusually productive mosaic for farming, fishing and fowling all at once.

There is no building stone. The material for monuments is the floodplain itself: some 55 earthen mounds at Cahokia, built basket-load by basket-load. Monks Mound, the largest, holds around 600,000 cubic metres of earth and covers a bigger footprint than the Great Pyramid.

The bluffs on the eastern edge are loess — wind-blown glacial dust — draining into the bottom through a set of creeks. That transition zone, wet bottom meeting dry upland, is where most of the population actually lived.

entries.title: Ice margin, then a long occupation
entries.body:
During the glacial maxima the ice sheet stops a little north of here; the Mississippi is a braided meltwater torrent and the climate is cold steppe.

After the ice retreats, people are in the valley continuously from Paleoindian times on — hunting, then adding native seed crops (goosefoot, marsh elder, little barley) that are domesticated in the midcontinent thousands of years before maize arrives. The Woodland-period communities here build burial mounds and trade in copper, marine shell and mica across half the continent.

entries.title: Maize, and the gathering
entries.body:
Maize, bred over centuries as it moved up from Mexico, becomes a staple in the American Bottom by around 900 CE — and the population climbs sharply.

Villages spread along the old channels and the creek mouths. The society is recognisably Mississippian in the making: settled maize farmers, ranked lineages, a religious life organised around platform mounds and open plazas. What has not happened yet is centralisation.

entries.title: The 'big bang' and the city
entries.body:
Around 1050 CE Cahokia is deliberately, rapidly rebuilt on a new plan — archaeologists call it the 'big bang' — and becomes the largest settlement north of Mexico, a distinction it holds until Philadelphia in the 1780s.

Estimates run from 10,000 to 20,000 people in the city and its immediate suburbs, more across the wider bottom. A 20-hectare Grand Plaza is levelled by hand at its centre; Monks Mound rises in stages on its north side; a stockade of some 20,000 logs later encloses the core. Standardised house-building, mass feasting deposits, and imported goods from the Gulf, the Appalachians and the Great Lakes all appear at once.

Mound 72 holds a burial of a high-status individual laid on a bed of more than 20,000 shell beads, alongside caches of arrows and the bodies of dozens of sacrificed young women — evidence of a hierarchy with the power of life and death.

entries.title: Coming apart
entries.body:
Within a century of its peak, Cahokia is emptying. By around 1350 the site is essentially abandoned, and stays that way.

No single cause is agreed. The stockade — rebuilt four times — points to chronic conflict. Deforestation of the uplands for fuel and palisades may have worsened local flooding; a drying climate after 1200 stressed the maize crop; and a political-religious order that demanded so much labour and display may simply have lost the consent it ran on. People dispersed into smaller, more egalitarian communities.

The 'ecocide' reading of Cahokia has been actively challenged; recent work finds less erosion and flooding than the older story assumed. Depopulation is certain; its drivers are not.

entries.title: The vacant quarter, and the interstate
entries.body:
When Europeans arrive the bottom is thinly populated — a buffer zone between later groups. The mound builders' identity is lost to outsiders, and the same racist reflex that met Great Zimbabwe attributes the earthworks to anyone but Native Americans.

The name 'Cahokia' is borrowed from an Illinois-confederacy band living nearby in the 1600s, not the builders, whose own name for the place is unknown. Nineteenth-century St. Louis is briefly nicknamed 'Mound City' before its mounds are carted away for fill.

Cahokia Mounds is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site — one of only a couple of dozen in the United States. U.S. Route 40 runs directly across it, and a subdivision covered part of the site before preservation caught up.

sources.text: Pauketat, T. — Cahokia: Ancient America's Great City on the Mississippi (Viking, 2009)
Emerson, T. E. & Lewis, R. B. (eds.) — Cahokia and the Hinterlands (Illinois, 1991)

aral.name: The Aral Sea
aral.subtitle: Endorheic basin between the Kyzylkum and the Ustyurt plateau
aral.geology:
How the ground got here

The Aral sits in a shallow tectonic depression with no outlet to the ocean — an endorheic basin. Two rivers fed it: the Amu Darya (the classical Oxus), off the Pamir and Hindu Kush, and the Syr Darya (the Jaxartes), off the Tian Shan. Water left only by evaporation, which is why the sea was mildly salty and why its level always tracked how much the rivers delivered.

That level has never been stable. Sediment cores show the Aral has shrunk and refilled many times over the Holocene, sometimes nearly drying out — often because the Amu Darya wandered, at times running west into the Caspian via the Uzboy channel instead of north into the Aral.

The exposed former seabed is now the Aralkum, the world's youngest desert. Its surface is loaded with salt and, in places, agricultural chemicals and residues from a Soviet bioweapons test site on a former island; wind lifts it in dust storms that carry hundreds of kilometres.

entries.title: A lake that comes and goes
entries.body:
Through the last glacial period the basin is cold desert; the rivers, fed by mountain ice, fluctuate wildly.

By the mid-Holocene the Aral is a substantial lake fringed by reed marsh and tugai forest along the deltas — prime habitat for fishing and hunting foragers, and later for the herders of the surrounding steppe. The deltas of the Amu and Syr, where fresh water spreads out before the salt, are the productive edge.

entries.title: Oxus civilisation and the first canals
entries.body:
The delta oases become the setting for some of Central Asia's earliest complex societies.

The Oxus civilisation (BMAC) of the Bronze Age builds fortified towns along the Amu Darya. In the Iron Age, Khwarezm — the irrigated land along the lower Oxus — emerges as a distinct polity with a dense network of canals and a string of mud-brick desert fortresses, the Elliq-Qala, whose ruins still stand in the Kyzylkum. Diverting river water for farming starts here, at a scale the land could absorb.

entries.title: Khwarezm: a name that meant water engineering
entries.body:
For over a thousand years the lower Oxus supports one of the great irrigation societies of the Islamic world, centred on Gurganj and later Khiva.

Khwarezm gives its name to the mathematician al-Khwarizmi — from whom 'algorithm', and via his book 'al-jabr', 'algebra'. The region is rich enough to be worth destroying: Genghis Khan sacks it in 1221, and the Mongols are said to have broken the dams and drowned Gurganj. The canals are rebuilt. The Aral, through all of this, stays roughly full — human water use is real but within the rivers' budget.

entries.title: Cotton, and the Russian plan
entries.body:
The Russian Empire annexes the region in the 1860s–70s and reorganises it around one crop: cotton, for Russian mills.

Irrigated area expands steadily under the Tsars and then dramatically under the Soviet Union, which treats Central Asian water as a resource to be fully allocated. Through the 1950s the Aral is still the fourth-largest lake on Earth, about 68,000 km², supporting a fishing industry that lands tens of thousands of tonnes a year from ports like Aralsk and Moʻynoq.

entries.title: The sea that was spent
entries.body:
From 1960 the Soviet Union massively expands cotton and rice irrigation — above all the leaky, unlined Qaraqum Canal drawing off the Amu Darya. Within a few years the rivers stop reaching the sea in most years.

The Aral falls off a cliff: by 2000 it has split into pieces; by 2014 the eastern basin — once open water to the horizon — is dry ground for the first time in 600 years. Salinity in what remains rises past the ocean's; the native fish die; the ports are left tens of kilometres from any shore, rusting trawlers on sand.

The northern lobe has partly recovered. A World Bank–funded dam, the Kokaral, completed in 2005, holds back the Syr Darya's flow; the North Aral Sea has risen several metres, cooled the local climate, and brought commercial fishing back to Aralsk. The much larger southern sea is generally considered beyond recovery.

This is often called the worst human-caused environmental disaster of the 20th century. That framing is widely accepted, but the water was diverted knowingly, for economic output that was real — it was a trade-off, not an accident.

sources.text: Micklin, P. — 'The Aral Sea Disaster', Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences 35 (2007)
Micklin, P., Aladin, N. & Plotnikov, I. (eds.) — The Aral Sea (Springer, 2014)
